summary: A Best Current Practice document that gives implementation recommendations for SMTP mail transfer agents so they can better reduce the impact of spam, for example by tightening how mail is relayed. It asks for discussion and suggestions for improvement.

eli5.summary: Junk mail floods the post office. This document tells the mail-sorting machines how to be stricter about who they carry mail for, so spammers can't use them for free.

subtitle: A 1999 checklist of anti-spam controls that every SMTP mail server should offer, starting with closing open relays.

tldr.problem: Spam was growing fast, costing receivers and ISPs real money, and spammers routinely hid behind third-party mail servers that relayed their mail for them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists 13 recommendations for SMTP Mail Transfer Agents: control relaying, keep traceable Received: lines and logs, block hosts or senders, limit mail rate, verify sender domains, restrict VRFY, EXPN and ETRN, and make return codes configurable.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 30), not a complete cure: the author says it only forces spammers into the open and buys time for a longer-term solution.

facts.label: Must never refuse
facts.value: The null sender and local-domain senders (section 2.6)

today: RFC 2505 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 30) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself says it is not the final solution to spam.

sections.title: The Spam Problem and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2505 is a Best Current Practice aimed at people who build SMTP Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs). Its goal is to make MTAs better at preventing and handling spam, and it also tells system administrators which "anti spam knobs" an MTA should have. It is not a guide to operating an MTA or to which knobs to turn.

The memo lists why spam is a serious threat: it is high volume, completely blind to what the receiver cares about, and it costs real money for receivers who pay for dial-up time and for ISPs. Its example is one 10 Kbyte message sent to 10 000 users at one ISP host, which means 100 Mbytes of unexpected storage. Many senders are also dishonest, using false return addresses and third-party hosts as relays.

The author is modest about the result. The rules, especially the Non-Relay rules, will not stop spam by themselves: even if 99% of SMTP MTAs adopted them, spammers would find the remaining 1% or connect directly to each recipient host. The hope is to get spammers out in the open, where legal action and technical blocking can reach them, and to give the community time to design a general solution. The memo restricts itself to IPv4.
sections.eli5: Junk mail is annoying and costs people money, and sneaky senders hide behind other people's mail machines. This memo cannot fix all of it, but it can make hiding much harder.

sections.title: The Thirteen Recommendations
sections.content:
Section 2 opens with a numbered list using the RFC 2119 words. An MTA MUST be able to restrict unauthorized relaying, add enough information to Received: lines to trace a message, keep local logs good enough to trace an event, and be configurable to give different return codes for different rules. It MUST NOT refuse MAIL From: <> or MAIL From: <user@my.local.dom.ain>.

An MTA SHOULD be able to log anti-relay and anti-spam actions, refuse mail from a host or group of hosts, refuse mail from a specific sender or a whole sender domain, rate-limit mail flow, verify the MAIL From: domain, verify the local part of outgoing mail, and control VRFY, EXPN and ETRN.

For matching hosts, domains and addresses, the memo recommends keeping the patterns in an external file and allowing regular expressions. Host and domain name matching MUST NOT be case sensitive, and the memo suggests treating the local part as case insensitive too. The overriding theme is flexibility, since spammers will find ways around any fixed rule.
sections.eli5: The memo is a checklist for mail machines: some things they must do, some they should do, and two kinds of mail they must never turn away.

sections.title: Controlling Mail Relay
sections.content:
An open mail relay lets strangers spend someone else's resources, puts the owner's reputation at risk and makes it impossible to filter spam without blocking legitimate mail. The memo points out that in an SMTP session, the HELO hostname and MAIL From: are easily and often forged. So relay decisions must rely on the RCPT To: domain, the caller's FQDN hostname and the caller's IP address.

The suggested algorithm has three steps. (a) If RCPT To: is one of the MTA's own domains, or a domain it agrees to forward for as an alternate MX, relay. (b) If the SMTP caller is authorized by IP address or FQDN, relay. (c) Otherwise refuse to relay.

Step (a) needs care: SMTP source routing, the % hack and uucp-style ! paths must be removed or accounted for before the test. A site should also take an inventory of gateways to other mail systems such as X.400 or DECnet MAIL-11 before turning on strict rules, because correctly addressed mail could be blocked. The configuration MUST support wild cards for FQDNs and classful IP addresses and SHOULD support address/mask for classless addresses.
sections.eli5: The mail machine asks three questions: is this mail for one of my own towns, is the sender someone I trust, and if neither, the answer is no.

sections.title: Tracing: Received Lines and Logs
sections.content:
Every MTA on the path, including the final one, MUST prepend a Received: line. It MUST contain the caller's IP address and the date-time. It SHOULD also contain the FQDN for the caller's IP address, the argument given in HELO, and authentication information if the connection was authenticated. The memo says these rules are deliberately stronger than RFC 1123, so that a spammer's dial-up IP address at a given time can be traced by the ISP.

Firewalls and gateways that hide an internal network may strip internal Received: lines, but they then take on full responsibility for tracing spammers inside. Incoming mail must keep its Received: lines intact, and a gateway SHOULD NOT change or delete them unless security requires it.

Logging follows the same idea. The MTA MUST keep enough local logs to trace an event, and SHOULD log all anti-relay and anti-spam actions, including the time, why the request was refused, the RCPT To: domains, and the offending host's IP and FQDN. The memo warns that more logging can open a denial of service path, since an attacker can fill logs with many RCPT To: commands.
sections.eli5: Every post office stamps the envelope and keeps a diary, so if bad mail shows up, someone can follow the stamps back to where it began.

sections.title: Refusing, Verifying and Limiting
sections.content:
An MTA SHOULD be able to accept or refuse mail by caller address: by FQDN, by wild card domain, by an individual IP address or by an address with a prefix length. Rules can be combined into a list that is searched until the first match. It SHOULD also be able to refuse a specific MAIL From: user or domain, which is easy for spammers to dodge but useful while an attack is going on. A rate control facility SHOULD slow mail sent or received, by throttling the TCP connection (reducing write() or read() frequency) or signalling a 4xx code.

Two senders must never be refused. MAIL From: <> is used for error messages from the mail system itself, and refusing it means users are not told about failures such as "User unknown". MAIL From: <user@my.local.dom.ain> is needed for aliases and forwarding, and for mailing lists, where RFC 1123 says the sender should be the list owner. The MTA MAY throttle MAIL From: <> mail with many recipients.

The MTA SHOULD check that the MAIL From: domain resolves to an MX or A record, and SHOULD allow outgoing local parts to be verified. The memo says VRFY and EXPN help spammers test and harvest addresses, so the MTA SHOULD control them. The default for EXPN and ETRN should be off, and for VRFY a 252 Argument not checked reply is suggested as the default.
sections.eli5: The post office can turn away mail from known troublemakers and slow down floods, but it must still accept bounce notices and mail that looks like it is from its own town, because honest mail uses those too.

sections.title: SMTP Return Codes
sections.content:
When an MTA refuses something, the first digit of the SMTP reply matters. 5xx is a permanent failure: the transfer ends and mail is returned to the sender. 4xx is a temporary failure: the mail is re-queued and tried later. 2xx means the MTA has taken responsibility for delivery.

The memo suggests 4xx for most cases, because a configuration mistake then delays mail instead of bouncing it. A 4xx also makes a spammer's own host fill up its queue, and a relay host full of queued spam is a sign something is wrong. The catch is MX records: if the lowest-preference MX refuses with 451, the sender may try the next MX host, which might accept the mail. Using a 2xx code and then discarding mail violates the intent of RFC 821 and should not be done without careful thought.

The MTA MUST be configurable to give 2xx, 4xx or 5xx per rule, but only the first digit should be configurable. If a DNS lookup gives a temporary failure, the MTA MUST answer 4xx; for an authoritative NXdomain it SHOULD still use 4xx but MAY be configured for 5xx. The memo's example is a university whose secondary MX host had to relay for its subdomains, which let it refuse relaying only for known spam sources, and only with a 4xx code.
sections.eli5: A "no, never" answer sends mail back for good; a "not now, try later" answer keeps it waiting. Waiting is safer if the post office might have made a mistake.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Side Effects
sections.content:
The security section describes spam itself as a risk: people can miss or delete important mail, ISP mail servers get overloaded and have crashed, and disk-full conditions can delay or lose mail. Relay hosts used by spammers are overloaded, and forged MAIL From: addresses blame innocent parties. Blocking spammers also risks blocking relay hosts that are themselves victims.

The methods in the memo have a cost too. They add load to DNS, logging, user databases and authentication systems, so sending spam to a site can become a denial of service attack on those support systems. The DNS checks add a specific risk: with negative caching, forged DNS responses could be used to block mail from chosen origins. The memo asks implementors to study how these systems behave under load, and states that a mail server MUST NOT respond with a permanent failure (5xx) when one of its support systems has a temporary problem.
sections.eli5: Checking everyone's name tag takes work, and a bully could flood the desk with visitors to jam it. So the post office has to be ready for that and say "try later" when its own helpers are busy.

sections.title: Future Work
sections.content:
The memo ends with ideas for a longer-term answer. Strict relay rules can hurt travelling users: a laptop on a dial-up pool or hotel network may get "Relaying Denied" from its home MTA. Workarounds include adding the network to the accepted list, using the current ISP's relay, or using the separate message submission profile of SMTP, RFC 2476. The memo also expects SMTP Authentication to add a rule to the relay algorithm: if the client is SMTP authenticated, accept to relay.

It also proposes per-user anti-spam filters with a system default that each user can override, while noting open questions such as how to explain 4xx and 5xx choices to ordinary users. Finally, it notes that when a NAT translates port numbers, logs would need port numbers as well as IP addresses to identify an inside host.
sections.eli5: Next steps are letting travellers prove who they are, letting each person set their own junk-mail rules, and keeping better notes when many computers share one address.
